kurz: How much of your wealth may fluctuate, and what this share is derived from.

bloecke.md:
In the euro series of the MSCI World from 1970 to 2025, the difference in return between a portfolio made up entirely of world equities and an entirely low-risk portfolio is around 5.7 percentage points a year. The largest setback is zero for the low-risk portfolio and 52% for the equity portfolio. Fund selection, entry timing or individual shares influence the result far less than the question of what share of your wealth may fluctuate.

Portfolio theory therefore separates two decisions that often coincide in everyday life. The first concerns the composition of the risky mix. According to the one-fund theorem, it is the same for all investors; it is covered in the lesson on the world portfolio. The second concerns how much of this mix you hold. This decision is individual, cannot be delegated and is the topic of this lesson. In this narrow sense, [[Asset allocation|asset allocation]] means setting the size of the risky share.

bloecke.titel: Return and volatility by equity allocation, 1970-2025
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with the MSCI World (net, euros) as the equity portion and a flat 2% p.a. for the low-risk portion, reset to the target allocation annually. Volatility grows in the same proportion as the allocation, whereas return grows ever more slowly, so the points lie on a curve that flattens towards the right.

bloecke.md:
## Purpose and building blocks of the low-risk portion

Low-risk here means nominally stable, available at short notice and without a price risk that materialises at the same time as losses on equities. In Germany, in September 2026, essentially three building blocks are suitable for this. The first are instant-access savings accounts and fixed-term deposits, whose interest rates are guided by the ECB deposit facility rate. By a decision of 10 September 2026, the ECB raised it to 2.50% with effect from 16 September 2026. The second are short-dated German federal bonds, with two-year bonds yielding 3.24% and five-year bonds 3.30% (Bundesbank yield curve, 18 September 2026). The third option is money market funds based on the €STR, whose return moves close to the deposit facility rate.

Statutory deposit protection covers €100,000 per customer and institution. After life events such as the sale of a home, an inheritance or a severance payment, it is up to €500,000 for six months. Compensation is to be paid within seven working days. Larger low-risk amounts are spread across several institutions or held in government bonds, whose creditworthiness does not depend on a single bank.

In real terms, this portion produces no return. With interest at 2.5% and inflation at 2.9% (August 2026), the result before tax is a loss of purchasing power of around 0.4% a year. Its purpose is the ability to act, that is, the possibility of not having to sell anything in a crash.

In 2022, the yield on ten-year Bunds rose from -0.21% to 2.53%, an increase of 274 basis points. By calculation, a ten-year zero-coupon bond bought at the start of the year lost around 22% by the end of the year. In the same year, the MSCI World fell by 12.8% in euros. From January 2008 to August 2026, the correlation of US equities with long-dated government bonds was -0.07, but in the inflation year 2022 it was clearly positive. For safety, it is therefore not enough to switch asset class; the maturity must also be short.

## Risk capacity, risk tolerance and need to take risk

[[Risk capacity]] is objective and can be calculated. It depends on the investment horizon, the security of income, the fixed-cost ratio, the size of the emergency fund and flexibility regarding your own goals. A single civil servant with a fixed-cost ratio of 30% has a different capacity from a self-employed woman with fluctuating orders and two children, regardless of how brave either of them feels.

[[Risk tolerance]] is subjective. It denotes the setback you can bear without selling. It can be read from your own behaviour in the last crash and from losses in euros rather than percentages, not from a questionnaire.

The [[Need to take risk|need to take risk]] is the third, usually overlooked quantity. It indicates how much risk the goal requires. If the goal can also be reached with 3%, there is no need to aim for 7%.

This leads to a rule for the allocation. The lower of capacity and tolerance limits the allocation, and need may lower it further. Capacity and tolerance must not be offset against each other.

bloecke.titel: Four situations from capacity and tolerance
bloecke.unter: A high allocation is only unproblematic in the top-right field; in the two mixed fields, the lower of the two quantities always determines the allocation.

felder.text: Short horizon or insecure income, but a high pain threshold. The most dangerous situation, because the pressure to sell comes from outside. The allocation must stay low.
Long horizon, secure income, emergency fund in place, setbacks have been endured before. The only remaining limit is the need to take risk.
Both quantities small. The low-risk portion dominates, and that is the right solution here.
Objectively a lot is possible, subjectively not. Raise tolerance gradually through experience or permanently accept a lower allocation. Panic selling costs more than the forgone premium.

bloecke.md:
## Liquidity needs and investment horizon

Liquidity needs come before the split. An [[Emergency fund|emergency fund]] of three to six months' expenses belongs in an instant-access savings account covered by deposit protection. It is typically needed precisely when prices are also low, and must therefore not be held in the portfolio. Added to this is every firmly planned expense over the next five years, such as a deposit for a property, the purchase of a car or an education. Only the amount left over after that is the subject of the allocation decision.

The investment horizon affects capacity, but less strongly than is often claimed. In the euro series of the MSCI World since 1970, 5 of 47 ten-year windows were negative, whereas all 42 fifteen-year windows were positive. The worst fifteen-year window returned 1.84% a year. This argues for long holding periods, but does not prove that shares become safe over time. With a longer horizon, the probability of a loss falls, whereas the possible size of the loss in euros grows with every year of saving. With a fall of 40%, a portfolio of €300,000 loses more money than one of €30,000, even though the percentage is the same.

bloecke.titel: Historical results by equity allocation (1970-2025, 56 years)

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation on a year-end basis with the same assumptions as above. The setback grows roughly in the same proportion as the allocation, whereas return grows ever more slowly. In addition, the setback occurs within a few years, while the return accrues over decades.

bloecke.md:
## Criticism of the “100 minus age” rule of thumb

The rule of thumb gives a 40-year-old 60% in equities and a 70-year-old 30%. It is easy to apply, but it is not derived from anything. Income, goal, horizon and expected volatility do not feature in it. The theoretically sound solution comes from Merton and Samuelson, and in it age plays no role.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula gives the Merton share for an investor with constant relative risk aversion. Age, wealth and remaining time horizon do not appear in it. Samuelson's objection to age-based rules of thumb rests on this.
variablen: expected return of the equity portion
risk aversion, usually assumed to be between 2 and 5
expected volatility of the equity portion
bloecke.beispiel: With μ = 6.5%, r = 2.5% and σ = 17%, γ = 2 gives an allocation of 69%, γ = 3 around 46% and γ = 5 around 28%. The 60% of the rule of thumb corresponds to γ ≈ 2.3. Because σ enters the formula squared, the allocation at γ = 3 falls to 33% if a volatility of 20% is assumed instead of 17%.

bloecke.md: The useful part of the age rule rests on human capital, that is, the value of future earned income, and not on age. A person with 25 years of secure salary ahead of them holds a large bond-like position outside the portfolio. They can therefore bear more equity risk in the portfolio. For the self-employed, employees in cyclical industries or people with shares of their own employer in their portfolio, on the other hand, human capital is equity-like. In that case the allocation should be lower, regardless of year of birth. The fact that the allocation falls in retirement follows from shrinking human capital and not from age as such.

## Calculating the need to take risk

The need to take risk can be calculated. €300 a month over 30 years adds up to contributions of €108,000. With the three model returns from above, before tax and costs this becomes around €209,500 (30% equities), €286,600 (60%) or €358,000 (85%). For a goal of €250,000, the middle allocation is sufficient, and the high one is not needed.

The calculation also works in reverse, and this case is often underestimated. If the goal can already be reached with existing wealth and low-risk interest, there is no longer any need to take risk. For this, Bernstein coined the phrase that you should stop playing once you have won the game. An inheritance, the sale of a business or a high salary late in life can therefore lower the right allocation, even if the person and their age stay the same.

bloecke.titel: Three profiles for orientation (not a recommendation)
zeilen: Horizon under 10 years or money already firmly earmarked
10-20 years, secure income, medium risk tolerance
over 20 years, secure income, emergency fund in place, market crash already experienced

bloecke.unter: The low-risk portion consists of immediately available instant-access savings for expenses and rebalancing and of short-dated euro government bonds for the rest. The emergency fund is not included in this calculation.

bloecke.md: Percentages seem harmless. With a portfolio of €200,000 and an equity allocation of 60%, the deepest setback in this model means minus 32.5%. That is around €65,000 less on the portfolio statement, spread over two to three years and accompanied by alarming headlines. With an allocation of 85%, it would be around €91,000. If such a loss is unbearable, the allocation is too high.

A single sheet should contain the target allocation, the permitted range and the occasions on which the allocation may be changed (change of job, inheritance, addition to the family, retirement, new goal). Market levels, forecasts and headlines explicitly have no place on it. Subsequent corrections cost money in Germany. Every sale triggers 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus solidarity surcharge, together 26.375% on the realised gain. For equity funds, the partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) of 30% reduces this burden. An allocation that is bearable from the start is therefore cheaper than any later correction.

When providing investment advice, the institution must carry out a suitability assessment under the Securities Trading Act (Wertpapierhandelsgesetz) and MiFID II. It covers knowledge and experience, financial circumstances including the ability to bear losses, investment objectives and risk tolerance. The result must be handed to the customer as a suitability statement (Geeignetheitserklärung). In practice, the questionnaire captures capacity only roughly and tolerance hardly at all. It serves mainly to protect the institution against liability and is no substitute for an analysis of your own situation. In execution-only business through an online broker, the assessment is largely omitted, and the classification is entirely up to the investor.

The equity allocation is the only quantity that determines both expected return and depth of loss at the same time. It is derived before the first purchase from capacity, tolerance and need, and not from market conditions.

mitnehmen: The split between the risky and the low-risk portion explains most of the result and the volatility, while product selection, by comparison, serves for fine-tuning.
The lower of objective risk capacity and subjective risk tolerance sets the upper limit of the allocation, and the need to take risk can lower it further.
Low-risk means short maturity and deposit protection and not simply bonds, because in 2022 long-dated Bunds lost more, by calculation, than the world equity index.
The “100 minus age” rule of thumb is not derived from anything, and the sound justification for falling allocations is shrinking human capital.
The allocation should be checked in euros, because a setback of 32.5% on €200,000 means a loss of €65,000, and you have to be able to bear that amount.

begriffe.text: The distribution of wealth across asset classes, in the narrower sense the ratio of the risky to the low-risk portion. It determines expected return and depth of loss more strongly than the selection of individual products.

The objectively measurable ability to bear losses. It depends on the investment horizon, security of income, fixed-cost ratio, emergency fund and flexibility of goals, regardless of how brave someone feels.
The subjective limit for losses, that is, the setback someone can bear without selling. It can be read more reliably from your own behaviour in the last crash than from a questionnaire.
The degree of risk needed to achieve the goal. If the goal is already secured, the need falls, and an additional equity allocation then brings more danger than benefit.

Three to six months' expenses in an instant-access savings account covered by deposit protection. The emergency fund stands outside the allocation calculation, because it is typically needed when prices are low.
